evidence: src/business/services/ReceivingService.ts: `async pick(sku: string, quantity: number, request?: Request)` puts the Express HTTP Request type (presentation/transport) into a domain method's signature.
src/business/services/ReceivingService.ts: `import { Request } from 'express';` exists only to support this transport-typed parameter.

src/business/services/ReceivingService.ts: `new Bin(data.code, data.sku, data.quantity, data.maxWeightGrams)` in pick() and bin(), and `new Item(d.sku, ...)` in item(), turn persistence records into domain objects (minor, infrastructure-leaning).
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
Most of ReceivingService is proper domain/application work. It validates that quantities are positive whole numbers, coordinates Bin.put and Bin.take, sums on-hand stock, and asks Item.needsReorder. Calling the injected tables to load and store data is normal service coordination.

The problem is pick(sku, quantity, request?: Request). This domain method takes Express's HTTP Request type as a parameter. That puts the transport framework into the domain service's public contract, and handling HTTP requests is the presentation layer's job. The parameter is never used, but it still ties callers of the domain operation to an HTTP framework. This is a mismatch between the file's role and its declared layer, separate from import direction. The controller should turn the request into plain values before calling the service.

A smaller point that I did not count as a violation: the private item() and bin() helpers, and the loop in pick(), build domain objects field by field from persistence records. That kind of record-to-object mapping usually belongs in the infrastructure layer.

violations.message: ReceivingService.pick takes `request?: Request` from Express. This puts an HTTP request type, which belongs to the presentation layer, into a domain service's contract. The controller should pull out plain values and pass those instead.
